title: East River Company Claim / Early Bushwick (1638)
summary: A 1638 agreement with named Native leaders gave the Dutch West India Company a claim along the East River. Company grants and later town-building changed control of a homeland now within Greenpoint and Williamsburg.

why_this_matters: A deed date alone hides the people, unequal power and consequences involved. Read the promises and removal demands alongside Native perspectives and continuing Lenape presence.
introduction_title: A Company claim over a Native landscape
introduction_content: A 1638 agreement with named Native leaders gave the Dutch West India Company a claim along the East River. Company grants and later town-building changed control of a homeland now within Greenpoint and Williamsburg.
history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
The Native landscape behind the later town name

The East River shore and the creeks toward Wallabout and Newtown belonged to a lived Native landscape. The 1638 record describes waterways and woods rather than a grid of city streets. The people named in it were dealing with places that supported their communities; the colonial name Bushwick and today’s neighborhoods came later. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

Who made the agreement, and who received the claim?

The instrument dated August 1, 1638 names Kakapoteyno, Menqueuw and Suwirau as chiefs of Keshaechquerem. It conveys the described tract for the benefit of the Dutch West India Company’s Amsterdam chamber. The Company was therefore the recipient, rather than one farming household. The written record claims the consent of the community, but that formula is not independent evidence of every resident’s understanding or agreement. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

What the written exchange contained

The record lists cloth, wampum, kettles, axes, hatchets and smaller goods. It describes land from George Rapalje’s plantation at Rinnegachonch toward Mespaechtes, extending inland from the East River to woods. Fernow’s notes identify Wallabout Bay and Maspeth Kill. The sweeping transfer language treated that landscape as property the Company could control. A goods list and signature date alone leave out the power and long-term consequences of that claim. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

From a Company claim to colonial settlement

The Company issued parcels to settlers after acquiring its claim. A later directive concentrated scattered settlers into a village in 1660; Stuyvesant named it Boswijck in 1661. Grants and town-building made the paper claim consequential through farms, house lots and local colonial authority. Broadway Triangle: general historical background

Read this place as part of a continuing history

This transaction is one part of Brooklyn’s history of land loss. Other agreements concerned different cultivated flats and shorelands; the 1652 Nayack record even required Native residents and descendants to leave. Those later events must not be mistaken for clauses of this 1638 deed. Follow the Brooklyn regional story for the distinct transactions and for Native-authored accounts of Lenape continuance and return. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

Continue with Brooklyn: Native Fields, Colonial Claims and Forced Removal.
whereintheworld_content:
This is an approximate 1638 claim landscape in today’s Greenpoint, Williamsburg and adjoining East Williamsburg. Fernow’s transcription describes the East River, Rinnegachonch and Mespaechtes, with inland woods. The Broadway Triangle historical assessment translates the tract into a later outline using Division Avenue, Broadway, Flushing Avenue and Newtown Creek. The map follows those modern street locators and the modern creek/river shore. Its eastern connection from Flushing Avenue toward the creek and woods is interpretive, not a surveyed deed line. Shore filling and creek alteration have changed the landscape. The outline represents the scale and setting of the Company claim, not the limits of Native homeland or proof that every person consented. It should not be read as today’s neighborhood of Bushwick, which has different boundaries.
